3. impl KernelFrame {
4.     /// Well-formedness of a kernel-frame handle: its owned physical address is page aligned.
5.     ///
6.     /// Purely structural — it makes **no** ownership claim (it does not assert that the frame
7.     /// is allocated). Page alignment is the one caller-visible fact `base()`'s consumers rely on:
8.     /// `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` index arithmetic behind it assume the returned
9.     /// `FrameAddress` is page aligned. Stated entirely on the abstract address `self@`, so it
10.     /// leaks no implementation detail. Mirror of `UserFrame::inv`.
11.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
12.         self@ % crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size() == 0
13.     }
14. }

4. //! Kernel frame type.
5. //!
6. //! A [`KernelFrame`] represents a single page-sized physical frame allocated for kernel use.
7. //! It provides `Deref`/`DerefMut` for direct kernel access (identity-mapped) and frees the
8. //! underlying frame on drop via the global frame allocator.
9. 
10. //==================================================================================================
11. // Imports
12. //==================================================================================================
13.

15. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
16. include!("kframe.spec.rs");

25. };

30. };

32. 
33. //==================================================================================================
34. // Kernel Frame
35. //==================================================================================================
36. 
37. /// A type that represents a kernel frame.
38. #[derive(Debug)]
39. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
40. pub struct KernelFrame {
41.     /// Frame address.
42.     base: FrameAddress,
43. }
44. 
45. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
46. verus! {
47. 
48. /// Abstract view of a kernel frame: the physical address of the owned frame.
49. impl View for KernelFrame {
50.     type V = int;
51. 
52.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
53.         self.base@
54.     }
55. }
56. 
57. } // verus!
58. 
59. // Dependency contract for the manager layer: wrapping a `FrameAddress` produces a handle whose
60. // abstract address is the same physical frame.
61. #[verus_verify]
62. impl KernelFrame {
63.     ///
64.     /// # Description
65.     ///
66.     /// Instantiates a kernel frame.
67.     ///
68.     /// # Parameters
69.     ///
70.     /// - `base`: Frame address.
71.     ///
72.     /// # Returns
73.     ///
74.     /// Upon success, a kernel frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
75.     ///
76.     // Dependency contract: wrapping a frame goes through `mm::virt::identity_map_page`, which
77.     // is outside the verification scope of `mm::phys`. On success the returned handle owns the
78.     // same physical frame that was passed in. `external_body` per `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`:
79.     // the identity-mapping side effect lives in `mm::virt` and the body's `?`/log closures call
80.     // into that layer, so the wrap contract is trusted until `mm::virt` is verified.
81.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
82.     #[verus_spec(result =>
83.         requires
84.             base.inv(),
85.         ensures
86.             match result {
87.                 Ok(kf) => {
88.                     &&& kf@ == base@
89.                     &&& kf.inv()
90.                 },
91.                 Err(_) => true,
92.             },
93.     )]
94.     pub(super) fn new(base: FrameAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
95.         // Ensure the frame is identity-mapped in the kernel address space so that
96.         // Deref/DerefMut can safely access it. This lazily installs a page
97.         // table entry if needed (page tables come from a BSS pool, so no recursive frame
98.         // allocation occurs).
99.         let phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> =
100.             PageAligned::from_raw_value(base.into_raw_value()).map_err(|e| {
101.                 error!("frame base is not page-aligned: {e:?}");
102.                 e
103.             })?;
104.         crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page(phys_addr).map_err(|e| {
105.             error!("failed to identity-map frame: {:?}", e);
106.             e
107.         })?;
108. 
109.         Ok(Self { base })
110.     }
111. }

115. 
116.     ///

118.     ///
119.     /// Returns the base address of the target kernel frame.
120.     ///

122.     ///
123.     /// The base address of the target kernel frame.
124.     ///
125.     // Pure accessor: returns the owned frame's physical address unchanged. `result@ == self@`

127.     // lets `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` arithmetic behind it proceed.
128.     #[verus_spec(result =>
129.         requires
130.             self.inv(),
131.         ensures
132.             result@ == self@,
133.             result.inv(),
134.     )]

137.     }
138. }

142.     ///
143.     /// # Description
144.     ///
145.     /// Clears the target kernel frame.
146.     ///
147.     /// Uses the identity-map `memset` backend so that the write runs in the kernel address space.
148.     /// This avoids a page fault when the current CR3 points to a user page directory that lacks
149.     /// the PDE for this frame's physical address.
150.     ///
151.     pub fn clear(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
152.         let base: *mut u8 = self.base.into_raw_value() as *mut u8;
153.         crate::mm::virt::memset(base, 0, mem::PAGE_SIZE).map_err(|e| {
154.             error!("memset failed: {:?}", e);
155.             e
156.         })
157.     }
158. }
159. 
160. /// # Safety
161. ///
162. /// `Deref` accesses the identity-mapped frame directly. The caller must ensure that the current
163. /// CR3 points to a page directory that has the relevant PDE for this frame's physical address
164. /// (i.e., the kernel page directory, or a user page directory into which the PDE has been
165. /// propagated via [`sync_kernel_pdes`](crate::mm::virt::sync_kernel_pdes)). For CR3-agnostic
166. /// writes, prefer [`KernelFrame::clear()`] which uses the identity-map `memset` backend.
167. impl Deref for KernelFrame {
168.     type Target = [u8];
169. 
170.     fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
171.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
172.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr as *const u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
173.     }
174. }
175. 
176. /// # Safety
177. ///
178. /// See [`Deref`] impl — the same CR3 invariant applies.
179. impl DerefMut for KernelFrame {
180.     fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Target {
181.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
182.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr as *mut u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
183.     }
184. }

191.     // `KernelStack::drop`) rely on this being the sole, complete deallocation step. Mirror of
192.     // `UserFrame::drop`.
193.     #[verus_spec(
194.         opens_invariants none
195.         no_unwind
196.     )]
197.     fn drop(&mut self) {
198.         if let Err(e) = super::frame::free(self.base) {
199.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
200.             error!("failed to free kernel frame: {:?}", e);
201.         }
202.     }
203. }

# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`

# Build Nanvix

Use this skill when the user asks to build, compile, format, lint, or spell-check Nanvix. This
covers all build-system operations exposed through the `z` utility.

## Prerequisites

- Development environment set up per `doc/setup.md`.
- A local cross-compilation toolchain (`toolchain/`).
- **Windows 11:** GNU Make on PATH, Windows Hypervisor Platform enabled,
  Developer Mode enabled, and Rust toolchain installed. See `doc/setup.md` for details.

## Windows Setup Summary

Before building on Windows, ensure:

1. **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All`, then reboot).
2. **Developer Mode** is on (Settings > Privacy & Security > For developers).
3. **GNU Make** is on PATH (`winget install ezwinports.make`).
4. **Rust toolchain** is installed via `winget install Rustlang.Rustup`.
5. Repository was cloned with `git clone -c core.symlinks=true`.
6. Git hooks are installed: `./z.ps1 setup`.

## Building

### Preferred Build Commands (using `z` utility)

```bash
# Build everything with the local toolchain.
./z build -- all
```

### Building Individual Components

```bash
# Kernel only.
./z build -- kernel
# Nanvixd only.
./z build -- all-nanvixd
# UserVM only.
./z build -- all-uservm
```

### Build Parameters

Set these as environment variables or pass them after `--` in the `z` command:

| Parameter        | Values                   | Default         |
|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| `MACHINE`        | `microvm`                | `microvm`       |
| `TARGET`         | `x86`                    | `x86`           |
| `RELEASE`        | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `LOG_LEVEL`      | `trace`, `debug`,        | `error`         |
|                  | `info`, `warn`,          |                 |
|                  | `error`, `panic`         |                 |
| `PROFILER`       | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `DEPLOYMENT_MODE`| `standalone`,            | `standalone`    |
|                  | `single-process`,        |                 |
|                  | `multi-process`, `l2`    |                 |

Example with custom parameters:

```bash
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=error
```

### Manual Build Variants

```bash
# Default debug build.
./z build -- all
# Release build.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic
# For echo-breakdown benchmark.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic TIMESTAMP_MSG=yes
```

### Building on Windows (using `z.ps1`)

On Windows 11, the `z.ps1` PowerShell script provides the same CLI interface. Guest components are
cross-compiled using a local toolchain; host binaries (`nanvixd`, `uservm`) are built natively with the
microvm backend (WHP on Windows).

```powershell
# Build everything (guest via make + host binaries natively).
.\z.ps1 build -- all

# Build only the UserVM (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- uservm

# Build only nanvixd (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvixd

# Build only nanvix-bench (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvix-bench

# Build only guest components (kernel + hello-rust-nostd).
.\z.ps1 build -- guest

# Release build.
.\z.ps1 build -- all RELEASE=yes
```

Any unrecognized target is forwarded to `make`, just like on Linux:

```powershell
.\z.ps1 build -- kernel
.\z.ps1 build -- format-check
.\z.ps1 build -- lint-check
```

## Code Quality

### Formatting

```bash
# Check formatting issues.
./z build -- format-check
# Auto-fix formatting issues.
./z build -- format
```

### Linting

```bash
# Check linting issues.
./z build -- lint-check
# Auto-fix linting issues.
./z build -- lint
```

### Spell Checking

```bash
# Check spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck
# Fix spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck-fix
```

## Formal Verification

Nanvix uses Verus for formal verification of selected kernel crates. The expected Verus version is pinned in `build/verus-version`. Verification requires `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to be set; when unset, `make verify` is a no-op.

```bash
# Install verus and run verification.
./scripts/setup/verus.sh ~/toolchain/verus
./z build -- verify VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus

# Verify a single crate.
./z build -- verify-bitmap VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus
```

- Set `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to the directory containing the `verus` binary.
- Use `scripts/setup/verus.sh <dir>` to download the pinned release.
- The `vstd` crate version in `Cargo.toml` is exact-pinned (`=`) to match the Verus binary.

## Cleaning

```bash
./z clean        # Clean build artifacts.
./z distclean    # Remove all generated files.
```

### Cleaning on Windows

```powershell
.\z.ps1 clean        # Quick clean (UserVM artifacts + cache).
.\z.ps1 distclean    # Full clean (cargo clean + all artifacts).
```

## CI/CD Pipeline

```bash
# Run the full CI pipeline locally.
./scripts/pipeline.sh
```

The pipeline covers: spell checking, formatting, linting, building, and testing across multiple
machine and deployment configurations.

## IDE Setup (Optional)

### Visual Studio Code

Use the host-specific settings template. The Linux template invokes `./z`, while the Windows
template routes Rust Analyzer through `./z.bat build -- check`, which runs native `cargo check`
on host crates (`uservm`, `nanvixd`, `nanvix-test`, `mkramfs`).

**Linux:**

```bash
mkdir -p .vscode && cd .vscode
ln -s ../scripts/setup/vscode/settings-linux.json settings.json
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .vscode -Force
Copy-Item scripts\setup\vscode\settings-windows.json .vscode\settings.json
```

> **Note:** The `check` target in `z.ps1` only checks host crates natively. Guest and kernel
> crates require the cross-compilation toolchain. Run
> `.\z.ps1 build -- check-kernel check-guest-binaries` for a full cross-target check.

## Troubleshooting Build Issues

- If builds fail with toolchain errors, verify `toolchain/` symlink points to a valid toolchain.
- Use `./z help` for usage information.
- **Windows:** Use `.\z.ps1 help` for Windows-specific usage information.
- **Windows:** If the UserVM build fails, verify that the Windows Hypervisor Platform feature is
  enabled (`Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform`).

690. /// # Errors
691. ///
692. /// - [`ErrorCode::InvalidArgument`]: Failed to read a valid paging entry.
693. ///
694. /// # Notes
695. ///
696. /// If the lazy mapper has not been initialized yet (boot page tables still active), this function
697. /// is a no-op and returns success.
698. #[verus_spec(result =>
699.     requires
700.         identity_map_view().inv(),
701.     ensures
702.         identity_map_view().inv(),
703.         match result {
704.             // The page containing `phys_addr` is reachable at its own physical address. After init
705.             // this means it is present (writable, supervisor) in the kernel page directory; before
706.             // init the call is a no-op and the boot page tables already cover it. Either way the
707.             // caller (`KernelFrame::new`) may subsequently read/write the frame through `phys_addr`.
708.             Ok(_) => identity_map_view().accessible(phys_addr@),
709.             // On failure the page was *not* made accessible, so `KernelFrame::new` must propagate
710.             // the error and must not dereference the frame. This is sound: an `Err` is only
711.             // reachable post-init (the pre-init path returns `Ok` as a no-op), and on the failure
712.             // path the page was not already mapped (an already-present PTE returns `Ok`) and the
713.             // failed `ensure_pt`/`ensure_pte` did not map it -- so `accessible` is false. Mirrors
714.             // the `mm::phys` convention of stating the failure-state fact over the global view.
715.             Err(_) => !identity_map_view().accessible(phys_addr@),
716.         },
717. )]
718. pub(crate) fn identity_map_page(phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>) -> Result<(), Error> {
719.     proof! { admit(); }
720.     let phys_addr: usize = phys_addr.into_raw_value();
721. 
722.     let pd_paddr: usize = KERNEL_PD_PADDR.load(Ordering::Acquire);
723.     // Check if the lazy mapper has been initialized.
724.     if pd_paddr == 0 {
725.         return Ok(());
726.     }
727. 
728.     let pde_idx: TableIndex = paging::pd_index(phys_addr);
729.     let pte_idx: TableIndex = paging::pt_index(phys_addr);
730. 
731.     // SAFETY: the PD is identity-mapped.
732.     let pd: Table<PageDirectoryEntry> = unsafe { Table::from_address(pd_paddr) };
733.     let pt_paddr: usize = ensure_pt(pd, pde_idx)?;
734. 
735.     // SAFETY: the PT is identity-mapped (BSS-backed).
736.     let pt: Table<PageTableEntry> = unsafe { Table::from_address(pt_paddr) };
737.     ensure_pte(pt, pte_idx, phys_addr)
738. }

476. # Count cfg-gated exec code (cheating indicator).
477. # When MODULE is set, counts only for module files; otherwise whole crate.
478. count_cfg_gates() {
479.     local scan_dir="$1"
480.     python3 -c "
481. import re, sys
482. from pathlib import Path
483. 
484. src_dir = Path('$scan_dir')
485. count = 0
486. cfg_pat = re.compile(r'#\[cfg(_attr)?\((not\()?verus_keep_ghost')
487. 
488. for rs_file in sorted(src_dir.glob('**/*.rs')):
489.     lines = rs_file.read_text().splitlines()
490.     for i, line in enumerate(lines):
491.         stripped = line.strip()
492.         if not cfg_pat.search(stripped):
493.             continue
494.         if 'derive(' in stripped or 'feature(' in stripped:
495.             continue
496.         target = ''
497.         for j in range(i + 1, min(i + 5, len(lines))):
498.             t = lines[j].strip()
499.             if not t or t.startswith('#['):
500.                 continue
501.             target = t
502.             break
503.         if any(target.startswith(k) for k in ['use ', 'use(', 'include!', 'extern ', 'mod ']):
504.             continue
505.         if re.match(r'(debug_assert|info|error|warn|trace|debug|log)!\s*\(', target):
506.             continue
507.         count += 1
508. 
509. print(count)
510. " 2>/dev/null
511. }
512. 
513. # --- Determine module-scoped cheating dir (if MODULE is set) ---
514. MODULE_CHEATING_DIR=""
515. if [[ -n "$MODULE" && -n "$CRATE_SRC_DIR" ]]; then
516.     if [[ "$MODULE" == "root" ]]; then
517.         MODULE_CHEATING_DIR=""  # root has no separate dir; skip module-scoped
518.     else
519.         MOD_CHEAT_PATH="${MODULE//:://}"
520.         # Collect the module file(s) into a temp dir for scoped scanning
521.         if [[ -f "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH.rs" || -d "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH" ]]; then
522.             MODULE_CHEATING_DIR="$(mktemp -d)"
523.             trap "rm -rf '$MODULE_CHEATING_DIR'" EXIT
524.             [[ -f "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH.rs" ]] && cp "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH.rs" "$MODULE_CHEATING_DIR/"
525.             if [[ -d "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH" ]]; then
526.                 cp -r "$CRATE_SRC_DIR/$MOD_CHEAT_PATH"/* "$MODULE_CHEATING_DIR/" 2>/dev/null || true
527.             fi
528.         fi
529.     fi
530. fi
531.

This means the only path to verify new's body is to have identity_map_view().inv() either as a precondition or baked into the manager's invariant chain. Let me step back and reconsider whether I'm overcomplicating this.

Looking at the source comment on new itself, it explicitly documents that the function is marked external_body because it calls into mm::virt::identity_map_page, which sits outside mm::phys's verification scope. The tcb-allowed.md notes that this will be verified when kframe is, but the source says it's trusted until mm::virt is verified. There's a slight tension there—identity_map_page does have a spec now with the precondition identity_map_view().inv(), but its body uses admit() and the broader mm::virt module remains unverified. So the real blocker is that precondition.

The core tension is that I could remove external_body from new if I add requires identity_map_view().inv(), but that would break the manager callers since they're verified and can't supply that invariant. Modifying manager is out of scope, so I need to find a precondition that new can impose while still letting manager's verified code call it. Let me check whether manager's own invariant or some global state already establishes identity_map_view().inv(), or whether there's a weaker relationship I can use instead of relying on identity_map_page's full precondition. Unless identity_map_view().inv() is provable in alloc_many_kernel_frames's context, adding that precondition to new would break the manager's and_then chain. Since the manager only has self.inv() and there's no global axiom asserting identity_map_view().inv(), I can't add this precondition without breaking code I'm not allowed to modify. This looks like a genuine dead-end for fully verifying new's body.

But wait — maybe I'm overcomplicating this. Let me check if there's prior art in the codebase showing how new was originally meant to be verified, or if there's an assume_specification mechanism that could thread the invariant through the manager's callers.
